articles.title: Cagayan Valley to test response to magnitude 8.5 quake in drill
articles.description: MANILA, Philippines — The government will again test its disaster preparedness on Thursday as emergency responders, local government units and communities simulate their response to a magnitude 8.5 earthquake and tsunami off Cagayan in yet another drill, the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) said. The full-scale exercise in Santa Ana, Cagayan, will simulate an earthquake triggered by movement along the East Luzon Trough, with the epicenter located 180 kilometers southeast of the coastal town. The simulation will be the highlight of the Fourth Quarter Nationwide Simultaneous Earthquake Drill (NSED) on November 5, which aims to assess the readiness of government agencies, emergency responders and communities to deal with a major earthquake and tsunami. The exercise will test the implementation of Santa Ana's Earthquake and Tsunami Contingency Plan and the Regional Disaster Response Plan of the Cagayan Valley Regional Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council. Among the response capabilities to be tested are early warning system activation, community evacuation, emergency telecommunications, search and rescue, mass casualty incident management and the activation of emergency operations centers. The drill will also simulate the management of evacuation camps and internally displaced persons, water search and rescue, management of the dead and missing, and responses to chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear hazards and oil spills. The OCD will lead the exercise in coordination with member agencies of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council and local government units. The NSED will begin at 8 a.m., with the ceremonial pressing of the button at 9 a.m. to signal the start of the nationwide "Duck, Cover and Hold" procedure and evacuation drills, followed by the full-scale simulation. Similar earthquake drills and related exercises will be conducted in other parts of the country under the supervision of OCD regional offices. The fourth-quarter exercise will also coincide with the observance of World Tsunami Awareness Day 2026, which carries the theme "Resilience Starts with You."

articles.title: Go pushes full implementation of disaster law
articles.description: SEN. Bong Go renewed his call for the full implementation of Republic Act (RA) 12076, or the Ligtas Pinoy Centers Act, and the creation of a Department of Disaster Resilience, after the Philippines topped a new global disaster risks survey. The 2026 World Risk Poll conducted by Gallup for the Lloyd’s Register Foundation showed that 80 percent of Filipino adults reported being personally affected by disasters in the past five years — the highest proportion among 140 countries surveyed. Tropical storms were the most cited hazard (52 percent), hitting 67 percent of respondents in the Visayas, while 44 percent of Mindanao respondents reported earthquake impacts. “We cannot prevent every disaster, but we can prepare for them. There must be safe evacuation centers, adequate equipment, a rapid response, and continuous support for the affected families,” Go said. Signed into law on Dec. 6, 2024, RA 12076, which Go principally authored, mandates the construction of permanent, disaster-resilient evacuation centers in every city and municipality to replace makeshift shelters such as public school classrooms. Coordinated by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, constructed by the Department of Public Works and Highways, and maintained by LGUs, these facilities require dedicated sleeping quarters, sanitation, healthcare areas, and emergency power and water systems. Go refiled Senate Bill 173 in the 20th Congress to establish the Department of Disaster Resilience. The proposed Cabinet-level agency would streamline risk reduction, emergency response, and recovery efforts across national and local agencies during large-scale calamities. Go also introduced SB 415 to provide rental housing subsidies for displaced families.

articles.title: Preparing for tsunamis
articles.description: THERE is a Japanese proverb that goes, “The next disaster strikes when the previous one has been forgotten.” On March 11, 2011, Japan experienced a 9.0-magnitude earthquake, also known as the Great East Japan Earthquake. Not only was it the most powerful earthquake to strike Japan, but it was also followed by a tsunami as tall as 40 meters, resulting in almost 20,000 deaths, an estimated $220 billion worth of economic damage, and a nuclear meltdown at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant. Nov. 5 is the United Nations’ World Tsunami Awareness Day. As we commemorate this international occasion, we must evaluate our preparedness for such kinds of natural hazards so that they do not become disasters. The unpredictable nature of tsunamis Tsunamis are not as common as typhoons. According to the US-based National Centers for Environmental Information, there have been 52 probable tsunami events in the Philippines from 1627 to 2024. In contrast, an average of 20 typhoons enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility every year, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa). However, tsunamis are much harder to predict. The event is usually triggered by submarine landslides, earthquakes or volcanic eruptions. Afterward, the waves travel through the ocean at high speed with a low amplitude that makes them unnoticeable on the surface. As the tsunami approaches coastal waters, the wavelength is compressed, and the amplitude grows drastically until the wave’s height towers over human settlements. Detection is the first line of defense Despite our technological advancements in engineering and architecture, we remain at the mercy of the forces of nature. We will never be able to build walls strong enough to withstand a tsunami. However, we are able to detect them in the propagation stage through a detection network. The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) has the tsunami early warning system, which makes use of gauge sensors to detect changes in sea level and water pressure in the event of seismic activity. This is critical because local tsunamis, which are generated within 100 kilometers of the source, can strike within two to five minutes after the trigger. Meanwhile, distant tsunamis originating outside the Philippines can take one to 24 hours before reaching our shores. Coordination is key We may have the most advanced detection systems, but none of that will matter if the warnings do not translate into action. This is where coordination between the national government and local government is crucial. Hazard planning is the foundation of disaster prevention. Local government units must create systems that guide citizens in the event of a tsunami. Where will people go? How will they reach evacuation centers? What will happen after the water recedes? In Japan, various communication channels are used to disseminate tsunami warnings, such as broadcasts on TV and radio and physical loudspeakers. Traditional means of communication are still important because we cannot assume that everyone has a smartphone and internet access. Planning and zoning for hazards Urban planning is a powerful tool in making our communities more resilient. We at Palafox practice what is known as ridge-to-reef planning where we treat everything, from the top of the mountains to the highlands, midlands, lowlands and coastal areas, as a single ecosystem. Nature does not recognize political boundaries, so we must ensure that our planning is comprehensive and integrated. Applying this principle, we can identify three zones with distinct purposes. The marine and coastal zone acts as the first line of defense, where coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass meadows and sand dunes dissipate the wave’s energy. The key term is “dissipate” because there is no single structure that can withstand the destructive force of a tsunami. According to the US-based Khaled bin Sultan Living Oceans Foundation, extensive mangrove areas can reduce the height of tsunamis by 5 percent to 30 percent, in addition to preventing erosion. Nature-based solutions must be complemented by infrastructure such as dikes, breakwaters and seawalls. The next area is the buffer and evacuation zone consisting of the lowlands and plains. Planners must conduct hazard mapping to ensure that critical infrastructure is situated outside of the inundation zone. Housing must also observe a coastal setback to keep people out of immediate danger. Circulation networks also play a pivotal role. People only have so much time before a tsunami strikes, so roads must provide direct access to evacuation routes. Meanwhile, waterways and estuaries must be unobstructed to ensure the smooth flow of water back to the sea. Lastly, the ridges and highlands are safe havens for people. Evacuation centers must be located inland and uphill with emergency shelters, communication hubs and medical supplies. Low-lying infrastructure may be damaged, so there must be an alternative source of food, water and supplies. Address hazards before they become disasters If the Japanese believe that “the next disaster strikes when the previous one has been forgotten,” I would like to respond with, “It is 90 percent less expensive to address hazards before they become disasters — in addition to saving human lives, property, livelihood, infrastructure and agriculture.” Given our location along the Pacific Ring of Fire, tsunamis are an ever-present risk for our coastal communities. However, we need not fear these hazards if we observe proper planning and preparation by working with nature, not against it. More than anything, tsunamis pose a leadership challenge for our public officials. Citizens cannot depend on the government alone, but it plays a critical role in ensuring that it uses its authority, resources and power to serve and protect its people. That is why we must support leaders who champion visionary leadership, strong political will and good governance.
